outcome: No accepted proof, disproof, or new bound on the conjecture itself appeared between 26 January 2024 and 11 October 2026. The one high-profile claimed disproof (an AI-assisted Lean project, 25 July 2026) was shown invalid by Lean's developer on 1 August 2026 because it exploited a kernel soundness bug. The rest of the window holds conditional reductions and partial density results (two Chang preprints, March 2026; Nwanozie, February 2026; Luo, 2025), finite verification to 2^71 (Bařina, journal 2025), and many self-published proof claims that no qualified reviewer was found to have examined.
problem_asks: The statement asks one universal claim: for every positive integer n, repeatedly applying the map (n even: n/2; n odd: 3n+1) eventually reaches 1, i.e. every trajectory terminates at 1. The statement names no separate parts. Standard consequences that a proof of the claim would also deliver, and that the statement does not list separately, are: no orbit diverges to infinity, and no non-trivial cycle exists. Alias: '3n+1 conjecture'.

events.what_happened: Terras showed that almost every positive integer (natural density 1) has a finite stopping time, i.e. its orbit eventually falls below its starting value. Recorded as background; the primary paper was not opened. The claim was taken from a 2025 ANTS XVII slide deck and the Wikipedia article's partial-results list, both seen only as search summaries.
events.delivers: Almost all starting integers (natural density) have a finite stopping time. This is a density-1 statement about typical n, not a statement about every n.
events.remains: Every orbit reaching 1; the stopping time of the exceptional density-zero set.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture in a density sense; no single orbit is shown to reach 1.

events.what_happened: Korec showed that for almost all m, the minimum value reached by the orbit is at most m^ε for ε > log 3 / log 4 (about 0.7925). Recorded as background from Inselmann's 2024 paper (opened) and a search summary of a 2025 slide deck; the 1994 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: A density-1 bound on the minimum of the orbit for typical starting values, with exponent just above log 3 / log 4.
events.remains: Every orbit reaching 1; the bound is for almost all m.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture in a density sense; not the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Krasikov and Lagarias showed that at least x^0.84 integers up to x eventually reach 1, for large x. Recorded from the Wikipedia article's partial-results list; the paper was not opened.
events.delivers: A counting lower bound on the number of integers up to x that reach 1. It is a count of successes, not a statement covering all n.
events.remains: All n up to x that do not reach 1 (none found); the remaining integers up to x.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture as a density-type count; not the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Simons and de Weger ruled out non-trivial cycles of length k for k up to 68. Recorded from the Wikipedia article's partial-results list; the paper was not opened.
events.delivers: No non-trivial cycle of length at most 68. A finite check of cycle lengths.
events.remains: Cycles of length above 68; divergent orbits; the conjecture.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture for cycles up to 68; a finite instance check.

events.what_happened: Hercher posted 'There are no Collatz m-Cycles with m ≤ 91' to arXiv (2201.00406, first version January 2022, title then 'm ≤ 90'). Published in the Journal of Integer Sequences 26 (2023), Article 23.3.5. A corrigendum to the proof of Theorem 21 exists (cs.uwaterloo.ca). The corrigendum date is not confirmed: the Wikipedia summary gives 14 June 2026, while the search could not confirm a 2026 date. Neither the arXiv paper nor the corrigendum was opened.
events.revisions: v3 April 2023 carries the 'm ≤ 91' title; corrigendum (undated in what I could see) to Theorem 21.
events.delivers: No non-trivial cycle of length m ≤ 91 for the 3x+1 map (i.e. m ≥ 92 for any cycle).
events.remains: Cycles of length 92 and above; divergent orbits; the conjecture.
events.doubts: The corrigendum says a derivation of one set of inequalities in the proof of Theorem 21 was wrong and offers an alternative route. Whether the main conclusion is affected was not established from the excerpt seen.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture for cycles up to length 91; a finite check.

events.what_happened: Kleinnijenhuis and Kleinnijenhuis posted 'Pruning the binary tree, proving the Collatz conjecture' to arXiv (2008.13643, v1 31 Aug 2020). The abstract describes pruning a binary tree of numbers until nearly 100% of naturals are removed, and says this proves the conjecture. The title and claim changed in later versions; the latest (v8, 26 April 2024) is titled 'The Collatz function as an automorphic Cayley colour graph: decidability of an+b conjectures, proof of the 3n + 1 conjecture' with a third author (Mustafa G. Aydogan). Versions 7 (11 Apr 2024) and 8 (26 Apr 2024) fall inside the window. I found no journal publication or referee report. The arXiv listing was opened for v1 and the current version; intermediate version titles come from a search summary.
events.revisions: v2 27 Oct 2020; v3 17 Jan 2021; v4 10 Dec 2021; v5 14 Jun 2022; v6 31 Mar 2023 (retitled, per search summary); v7 11 Apr 2024; v8 26 Apr 2024 (latest; retitled as above; third author added).
events.delivers: Claimed: that the pruning removes all but a density-zero set of naturals, from which the authors infer that every starting integer reaches 1. The abstract as read does not show why density of removed numbers implies convergence for every n.
events.remains: Every starting integer reaching 1, per the claimed argument's own step; the claimed step is not visible in the abstract as read.
events.time_since_posted: 6 years 1 month (v1, Aug 2020); latest version April 2024
events.directly_checkable: The authors provide a Mathematica notebook as ancillary material, per a search summary; not opened.
events.doubts: The argument's key inference (density of unpruned numbers goes to zero implies every orbit reaches 1) is not shown in the abstract. The title and the claimed result changed across versions. No journal publication or referee report was found in searches. The authors' own abstract refers to the conjecture as yet unproven.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture for all n.

events.what_happened: Terence Tao posted 'Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values' to arXiv (1909.03562, v1 8 Sep 2019). The main theorem: for any function f with f(N) → +∞, Col_min(N) ≤ f(N) for almost all N in logarithmic density. Published in Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), e12, 56 pp. The arXiv listing shows v6 (6 Jul 2026) and v7 (16 Jul 2026); I did not examine what changed in those versions.
events.revisions: v2 13 Sep 2019; v3 7 Jun 2020; v4 18 Sep 2021; v5 15 Feb 2022; v6 6 Jul 2026; v7 16 Jul 2026 (2026 changes not examined); journal publication Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), e12.
events.delivers: For almost all N (logarithmic density), the minimum of the Collatz orbit is at most f(N) for any f diverging to infinity. A measure-theoretic statement that almost all orbits dip arbitrarily low. It does not show any orbit reaches 1.
events.remains: Every starting integer reaching 1; the exceptional set of density zero; whether the minimum equals 1 for any particular n.

checked_by.who: Forum of Mathematics, Pi (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), e12)

events.direction: Toward the conjecture in a measure-theoretic sense; does not reach 1.

events.what_happened: Chin-Long Wey posted 'The Proof of the Collatz Conjecture' (arXiv 2309.09991, math.GM, v1 15 Sep 2023). The abstract builds a tree of inverse Collatz and Syracuse steps rooted at 1 and proposes a 'PathFinding' algorithm to find a path from any starting number back to 1, stated as intended 'to prove both Syracuse and Collatz conjectures'. The abstract calls the problem 'still unsolved'. v2 (16 Feb 2024) and v3 (13 Jun 2025) fall inside the window.
events.revisions: v2 16 Feb 2024; v3 13 Jun 2025 (current).
events.delivers: Claimed: a path from every starting number to 1 via the tree. As read from the abstract, no completed argument for the path's existence is visible.
events.remains: Every starting number reaching 1; the Syracuse conjecture as well.
events.doubts: The title asserts a proof while the abstract frames the work as a method and calls the problem unsolved. No verification, referee report, or commentary was found in searches. Only the abstract was read.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture (per title); the abstract is ambiguous on whether it does.

events.what_happened: Yolcu, Aaronson and Heule posted 'An Automated Approach to the Collatz Conjecture' (arXiv 2105.14697, v1 31 May 2021; v2 20 Aug 2022; v3 31 Dec 2022). They build a string-rewriting system on mixed binary-ternary representations whose termination is equivalent to the conjecture, and use a minimal termination prover (matrix interpretations) to prove some non-trivial weakened versions automatically. The abstract as read states the authors do not prove the conjecture itself.
events.delivers: An equivalence: termination of the proposed rewriting system is equivalent to the Collatz conjecture. Automatic proofs of weakened versions. The equivalence is a reformulation; no instance of the full conjecture is settled.
events.remains: The full conjecture.
events.direction: Reformulation; neither confirms nor refutes the conjecture; proves weakened variants.

events.what_happened: Duan, 'A Solution to the Collatz Conjecture Problem', on Preprints.org (manuscript 202301.0541; the month is inferred from the manuscript ID). Version 17 is dated 2 October 2024, per a search summary. The page returned HTTP 403 and was not opened. The claim (a modified odd-number operation and a tree model) is taken from a search summary.
events.revisions: Many versions; v17 2 Oct 2024 (per search summary).
events.delivers: Claimed solution of the conjecture; not checked.
events.remains: Unknown; not checked.
events.doubts: Preprints.org labels its versions not peer-reviewed (per search summary). Not opened, so no argument was read.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Manuel Inselmann posted 'An approximation of the Collatz map and a lower bound for the average total stopping time' (arXiv 2402.03276, v1 5 Feb 2024; v3 13 Aug 2024). Its results concern typical integers and averages; the paper states they are meaningful only if the conjecture holds, and does not prove it.
events.revisions: v2 (date not seen); v3 13 Aug 2024.
events.delivers: Unconditional: for almost all m, the trajectory stays near the envelope (√3/2)^k m^(1±ε) up to k about 6.952 log m; for almost all m, the minimum T_min(m) ≤ m^ε for any ε>0, improving Korec; liminf of the average total stopping time over m ≤ x, normalised by x log x, is at least 2 / log(4/3). Conditional: if τ(m) = O(log m) for all m, that average converges to the same constant.
events.remains: Every starting integer reaching 1; the results cover typical integers and averages only.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture in density and average senses; not the conjecture.

events.what_happened: E. Diedrich posted 'Resolution of the Collatz Conjecture: A Rigorous Analysis of Collatz Sequences and their Unique Cycle' on Preprints.org (manuscript 202406.0256). Its abstract claims a Bounded Subsequence Property and uniqueness of cycles, and a complete resolution: all Collatz sequences reach the cycle {1, 4, 2}. Version history per a search summary: v1 5 June 2024; v6 13 Aug 2024; v7 19 Aug 2024 retitled 'The Collatz Conjecture: A Resolution through Inverse Function Generative Completeness'. A related February 2025 Diedrich preprint ('A Proof Through Inverse Generation Analysis') is per search summary only. The Preprints.org page returned HTTP 403 and was not opened.
events.revisions: v6 13 Aug 2024; v7 19 Aug 2024 (retitled); per search summary.
events.delivers: Claimed complete resolution: every Collatz sequence reaches {1, 4, 2}. Not checked.
events.remains: Nothing is established on the evidence I could read.
events.doubts: Preprints.org labels the versions not peer-reviewed (per search summary). The abstract itself asks for peer review and verification by the community. No acceptance by the community was found in searches. Not opened.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture is true for all n.

events.what_happened: Budee U. Zaman, 'Revealing a Binary Pattern Validates 3n+1 Problem for All Positive Integers' (Preprints.org manuscript 202404.0943; also EasyChair). The search summary says the author claims a proof. The pages returned HTTP 403 and were not opened.
events.delivers: Claimed proof; not checked.
events.remains: Nothing is established on the evidence I could read.
events.doubts: Preprints.org marks the version not peer-reviewed (per search summary). Not opened.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture is true.

events.what_happened: Saleh Omran posted 'On the Collatz conjecture' to Cambridge Open Engage (Working Paper, version 1 on 12 July 2024; version 2 on 2 August 2024). The abstract says the author 'suggest[s] a proof for 3n+1 problem', stating 'We proof that the k-th iterate of Collatz function C^k(n) is bounded for all positive integer numbers k; n and converges to 1.' The page says the work has not been peer-reviewed by Cambridge University Press; no reviewer comments are shown.
events.revisions: v2 2 Aug 2024 (not reviewed).
events.delivers: Claimed: the iterates are bounded for all k and converge to 1 for all n. That is the full conjecture, as claimed. The argument is not visible in the abstract.
events.remains: Nothing is established on the evidence I could read.
events.doubts: The claim that the iterates are bounded for all k is the core of the conjecture, asserted without a visible argument in the abstract. Not peer-reviewed; no comments shown on the page.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture is true.

events.what_happened: A six-state Turing machine, the 'antihydra', was found in July 2024 whose halting depends on a Collatz-like problem, in busy beaver research. Recorded from the Wikipedia article's 2024 entry; not opened.
events.delivers: Not a result on the conjecture: it relates the halting of a specific machine to a Collatz-like problem.
events.remains: The conjecture, and the status of the machine's halting.
events.direction: Not about the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Abderrahman Bouhamidi, 'Two general and curious conjectures like Collatz's' (HAL hal-04559567, 2024). It sets up a family indexed by p ≥ 0 (d_p = 2^p+1, α_p = 2^p+2, β_p = 2^p) and conjectures that the process always reaches 2^p; the classical Collatz conjecture is the case p = 0. Opened only via search summary.
events.delivers: Conjectures only; no result is proved.
events.remains: All of it, for the classical case.
events.direction: Proposes a family of analogues; not a result on the conjecture.

events.what_happened: David Bařina, 'Improved verification limit for the convergence of the Collatz conjecture', The Journal of Supercomputing 81(1), 1–14 (DOI 10.1007/s11227-025-07337-0). The paper verifies convergence for all starting values up to 2^71, with a 1,335× speed-up from the first CPU algorithm to the best GPU algorithm, run on thousands of parallel workers across European supercomputers, and reports four new path records. Accepted 21 April 2025; release 2 May 2025 per a Brno University record. Springer's page redirected to a login and was not opened; the figures come from the university record and the Wikipedia article.
events.revisions: Earlier verification in Bařina 2021 (Journal of Supercomputing 77(3)) and the 2020 bound 2^68 per a search summary of the project page.
events.delivers: Verification that every starting value up to 2^71 reaches 1. A finite range of instances of a universal claim. It does not reach any n above 2^71.
events.remains: Every n above 2^71; the conjecture as a universal claim.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the computational verification paper for publication (accepted 21 April 2025, per the Brno record)

events.directly_checkable: The verification is a computation over a finite range; the code and its checking were not examined.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the range checked; no counterexample found below 2^71.

events.what_happened: Youchun Luo, 'Iteration Steps of 3x+1 Problem' (arXiv 2506.23070, math.GM, v1 29 June 2025; v2 11 July 2025; v3 16 July 2026, comment: 'qx+1 situation added'). The abstract proposes a Weak Residue Conjecture, 2^E(N) / (3^O(N) · N) < 2, and proves that if the 3x+1 conjecture and this conjecture are both true, the step counts D(N), O(N), E(N) satisfy relations such as O(N) = ⌊log_6 2·D(N) − log_6 N⌋. The search summary says the paper was 'published online August 6, 2026' per a Lean project README; I could not locate that journal version.
events.revisions: v2 11 Jul 2025; v3 16 Jul 2026 (adds the qx+1 case).
events.delivers: Conditional on the 3x+1 conjecture and the Weak Residue Conjecture: nontrivial relations among the total, odd and even step counts. It does not prove the conjecture or the Weak Residue Conjecture.
events.remains: The 3x+1 conjecture itself; the Weak Residue Conjecture (assumed).
events.doubts: Both results are conditional on assumed conjectures; the Weak Residue Conjecture is itself unproven. No referee report or independent check was found.
events.direction: Conditional relations between step counts; neither confirms nor refutes the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Abderrahman Bouhamidi, 'An Extension of the Collatz Conjecture modulo 2^p+2^q' (arXiv 2601.06208, submitted 8 January 2026; the PDF front page is dated 5 November 2025). Proposes a general conjecture that contains the classical Collatz conjecture and an example modulo 10 conjectured to end at 4. Conjectures only; opened only via search summary.
events.delivers: Conjectures only.
events.remains: All of it.
events.direction: A family of analogues; not a result on the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Abderrahman Bouhamidi, 'Weakly and Strongly Admissible Triplets for a Collatz-Type Map' (arXiv 2601.17573, submitted 24 January 2026; the PDF header is dated 11 November 2025). It defines weak and strong admissibility of triplets and restates the classical conjecture as a claim that one triplet is strongly admissible. Opened only via search summary.
events.delivers: A framework and conjectures for a family of maps; the classical case is restated, not proved.
events.remains: All of it, for the classical case.
events.direction: Reformulation for a family; not a result on the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Barmak Honarvar Shakibaei Asli, 'An Explicit Near-Conjugacy Between the Collatz Map and a Circle Rotation' (arXiv 2601.04289, math.GM, submitted 7 January 2026). The logarithmic transform makes the map a circle rotation by log_6 3 with bounded error |ε(x)| ≤ 0.2749, with numerical checks to 10^12. The paper states: 'While this near-conjugacy does not by itself resolve the Collatz conjecture.'
events.delivers: An approximate conjugacy with bounded error for all positive integers, as claimed. It does not resolve the conjecture by its own statement.
events.remains: Every orbit reaching 1; a bounded error does not give termination.
events.directly_checkable: Numerical checks up to 10^12 are described; code not examined.
events.direction: Partial and approximate; the paper disclaims resolving the conjecture.

Describes an algorithm that verifies convergence for all n < 2^N for a fixed N; going from 2^N to 2^(N+1) takes less than twice as long. The abstract names no specific N and makes no claim to prove the full conjecture; it also discusses the analogue for negative numbers.

events.what_happened: Kevin Nwanozie, 'A Rigorous Framework for the Collatz Conjecture' (Cambridge Open Engage, DOI 10.33774/coe-2026-z2kb7; Working Paper, version 1 on 10 February 2026). The abstract restricts attention to odd N with v2(3N+1) ≤ 6, which the author says contains 63/64 of odd integers, and claims to prove that this restricted problem is equivalent to the full conjecture. It also characterises the set by congruences, gives growth constraints, develops Markov models, and connects to Tao's 2019 result. Not peer-reviewed; no reviewer comments are shown.
events.delivers: Claimed: the restriction to odd N with v2(3N+1) ≤ 6 is equivalent to the full conjecture. The equivalence is the entire claimed content of the abstract.
events.remains: The remaining 1/64 of odd integers, the even integers (unless the claimed equivalence covers them), and the equivalence step itself, which is not visible in the abstract.
events.doubts: The abstract does not show how an equivalence for 63/64 of odd integers extends to the other 1/64 or to even integers. Not peer-reviewed; comments section empty. The author declares no competing interests and the content is CC0.
events.direction: Claims an equivalence reducing the conjecture to a restricted set; the claimed proof of the equivalence is not visible.

events.what_happened: Jennifer Williams, 'A Coordinate System for Collatz Dynamics' (arXiv 2607.01718, math.NT, submitted 2 July 2026; one version). The paper partitions the non-negative integers into triangles indexed by a 3-smooth factorisation and proves that rows k ≡ 2 (mod 4) with k ≥ 6 in the principal skeleton L_1 contain no primes. The abstract states 'with all results independent of the Collatz conjecture.' The comment field says '21 pages, 5 figures, under peer review.' The authors' disclosure (in the HTML rendering) names an AI tool used in drafting; see the ai field.
events.delivers: Partial structural results on a coordinate system, including a no-primes result for one residue class of rows. The author says the results are independent of the conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture; the paper does not bear on it by its own statement.
events.doubts: Under peer review per the comment field; the venue is not named. No engagement found.
events.direction: Does not bear on the conjecture by the author's own statement.

events.what_happened: Edward Y. Chang, 'Exploring Collatz Dynamics with Human-LLM Collaboration' (arXiv 2603.11066, math.DS, v1 10 March 2026; v6 22 April 2026 is current). The first-page abstract (HTML v6) says the paper 'is not a proof of the Collatz conjecture; it characterizes why the conjecture resists proof'. It claims unconditional results: a uniform spectral gap for the Syracuse transfer operator, a density-0 result for divergent starting points, and a cylinder-averaged density-1 convergence result. It names the 'Distributional-to-Pointwise Gap' as the irreducible core. v2 (17 March 2026) introduced the Weak Mixing Hypothesis as the primary open condition (per search summary; not read in the text). The arXiv metadata abstract names no AI system; the first-page abstract does (see ai field). Section 12 (the contribution analysis) could not be retrieved from the cached PDF or HTML.
events.delivers: Claimed unconditional: a uniform spectral gap for the Syracuse transfer operator; a density-0 bound on divergent starting points; a cylinder-averaged density-1 convergence result. These are statements about almost all starting values or about measure, not about every n. The author states the reduction of the pointwise statement to the Distributional-to-Pointwise Gap.
events.remains: The pointwise statement for every starting integer (the Distributional-to-Pointwise Gap, which the paper says is equivalent to the divergence component); and, per the v2 framework, the Weak Mixing Hypothesis.
events.doubts: The paper itself locates the open gap at the pointwise level. A search summary of the companion paper says the author concedes that solving the Weak Mixing Hypothesis is 'in all likelihood, essentially as hard as the Collatz conjecture itself'. Single author; no independent verification found; SOTAVerified lists it as unverified (search summary).
events.direction: Toward the conjecture in distributional and density senses; the paper explicitly disclaims a proof of the pointwise conjecture.

events.what_happened: Edward Y. Chang, 'A Structural Reduction of the Collatz Conjecture to One-Bit Orbit Mixing' (arXiv 2603.25753, math.DS, submitted 24 March 2026; one version). It reduces the conjecture to a fixed-modulus, one-bit orbit-mixing problem. Its results: exact low-depth decomposition formulas at depths K = 3, 4, 5; a Map Balance Theorem (for K ≥ 5 the counts of burst residues mapping to gap starts ≡ 3 and ≡ 7 mod 8 differ by exactly 1); and, for the dominant n ≡ 1 (mod 8) class, a gap outcome that depends on bit 4 of the orbit value at burst-ending times. The conjecture is reduced to whether every orbit visits two residue classes modulo 32 with 'sufficient balance along a sparse subsequence'; the abstract does not define 'sufficient balance'.
events.delivers: A claimed reduction of the conjecture to an orbit-mixing condition (sufficient balance along a sparse subsequence in two residue classes mod 32), plus the Map Balance Theorem and low-depth formulas. The reduction is not a proof; the balance condition is open.
events.remains: The orbit-level balance condition, which the abstract does not define; the conjecture for every n.
events.doubts: The balance condition is undefined in the abstract as read. Two search summaries differ on whether the reduction is conditional (the fetched HTML summary) or unconditional (a search summary, which says the open part is the deterministic orbit-level balance statement). Both readings point at the same open condition. Single author; no independent verification found.
events.direction: Reduction to a balance condition; no proof either way.

systems.name: MACI framework
systems.what_it_did: Named as the 'Human–LLM collaborative research platform' on which the paper was developed. No model is named in this paper; the paper defers 'the full methodology, disclosure of AI tool usage, and verification procedures' to the companion paper 2603.11066. What the platform did in this paper is not stated.
systems.basis_quote: This paper was developed using the Human–LLM collaborative research platform described in the MACI framework [4, 5].

events.what_happened: Ramana Kumar (GitHub xrchz) published the Lean 4 repository 'Collatz conjecture in Lean' (github.com/xrchz/CollatzLean) on 25 July 2026, with two commits that day: 2f19c9f 'Initial commit, playing around with Collatz ideas' and a793574 'Finish disproof'. The README claims existence rather than a specific counterexample: Collatz.exists_nonterminating_orbit : ∃ n, Collatz.Diverges n, and Collatz.not_conjecture : ¬ Collatz.Conjecture. It says the argument is witness-free, and that it was checked by the Lean kernel and independently by Nanoda (pinned, with no permitted axioms); Lean and Mathlib are pinned to v4.32.1. On 28 July Kiran Gopinathan reduced the exploit to a small proof of False and opened Lean issue #14576. The fix (#14577) was merged within about an hour; Lean 4.32.2 was released 28 July. A separate Nanoda bug (reported by Jeremy Chen, fixed about a week earlier) was also involved. Leonardo de Moura's postmortem (1 August 2026) states that the proof is not valid: the kernel accepts a proof of False through a bug in its handling of nested inductive types with phantom parameters, reachable through metaprogramming. Paulson (30 July 2026) also reported the proof as wrong.
events.revisions: Kernel fix #14577 and Lean 4.32.2 (28 July 2026); Nanoda patched; postmortem 1 Aug 2026. The repository itself was not seen to change after 25 July 2026.
events.delivers: As submitted: a claimed proof that a non-terminating orbit exists, which would make the conjecture false as formalised. As established by the postmortem and the Paulson post: nothing valid. The proof exploits an implementation bug in the Lean kernel and proves False.
events.remains: The whole conjecture: no valid proof or disproof is established by this event.

The postmortem quotes that Kumar 'believes the timing was coincidental, but cannot rule out that the model had seen the nanoda report'. A LessWrong post reported in a search summary says Kumar knew of the bug at publication; that post was not opened. No withdrawal by the author was found in any source I opened.

events.object: A witness-free Lean existence proof: ∃ n, Collatz.Diverges n, meaning some starting integer has an orbit that never reaches 1. No specific n is given, so the object is non-constructive. The postmortem says the argument established False via the kernel bug, so the existence claim carries no weight.

events.what_happened: A public repository, antidepersonalizationer/wrc-lean (5 commits, 0 stars; no first or latest commit date visible on the page), labelled 'AI-GENERATED / AI-ASSISTED RESEARCH ARTIFACT'. It contains a Lean 4 proof of a residue bound: for all n and k, FirstHit n k implies residual n k < 2, where Res = 2^k / (3^s · n) (WRC.wrc : WRCStatement). It also proves exact identities for D, O and E for trajectories that first reach 1. The README says the project 'does not prove global Collatz termination or the strong residue conjecture'. The recorded full check completed 23 September 2026, 10:53 UTC. Toolchain leanprover/lean4:v4.20.1; the README says the audit rejects sorryAx and reports only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
events.revisions: Five commits; dates not visible. The 23 Sept 2026 date is the recorded check run, not a posting date.
events.delivers: Lean-verified: for every n and k such that the trajectory first hits 1, the residue quantity 2^k/(3^s·n) is below 2. This is the inequality of the Weak Residue Conjecture of Luo (arXiv 2506.23070) restricted to trajectories that reach 1. It establishes nothing about whether a trajectory reaches 1.
events.remains: Global termination (every n reaches 1); the strong residue conjecture; the unrestricted Weak Residue Conjecture for n that do not first hit 1 (a hypothesis of the theorem excludes them).

The article says the proof is hundreds of pages long, that the full details have not been published, and that mathematicians have begun verifying it. It names no model and gives no link to an OpenAI announcement, paper, or the Ars article. The Ars Technica article was not found in searches. The English version of the same site says OpenAI's mid-May 2026 announcement concerned the Erdős unit distance conjecture, not Collatz. I could not verify the June claim.

disputes.summary: Who found the Lean kernel bug behind the CollatzLean 'disproof'. Tao's 9 October 2026 guest post says 'The Collatz bug was found by Ramana Kumar, a co-author of' (a named work), and that the bug 'was not caught by cross-checking against a somewhat out-of-date Nanoda kernel'. The postmortem, as quoted in secondary sources, says Kiran Gopinathan reduced the exploit to a small proof of False and opened issue #14576 on 28 July 2026. Gigazine says Kumar found the Lean bug while investigating the counter-argument, after publishing the repository. Not resolved here.

Whether the author knew of the kernel bug when publishing. The postmortem (as quoted) says Kumar 'believes the timing was coincidental, but cannot rule out that the model had seen the nanoda report'. A LessWrong post, seen only in a search summary, says Kumar's result was circulated as a Collatz proof while he knew it exploited a soundness bug. Kumar's own account was not found.

Whether the Chang companion paper (2603.25753) reduction is conditional or unconditional. The fetched HTML summary calls it conditional, on 'sufficient balance along a sparse subsequence'. A search summary of the abstract says the author states the reduction is unconditional, and that the open part is the deterministic orbit-level balance statement. The two readings agree on the same open condition.

AI disclosure for Chang 2603.11066: the arXiv metadata abstract names no model ('Produced through human-LLM collaboration; see Section 12'), while the first-page abstract in the HTML version names 'Claude 4.6 (Anthropic)' and 'GPT 5.4 Thinking (OpenAI)'. The HTML text was read across two fetches with the same result. Recorded as a discrepancy; not a priority dispute.

The June 2026 OpenAI Collatz claim. The winzheng English article says OpenAI's mid-May 2026 announcement concerned the Erdős unit distance conjecture; the Chinese article attributes a complete Collatz proof to OpenAI on 1 June 2026, citing an Ars Technica report that could not be found. Both articles are secondary; no primary source found.

summary: Across 26 January 2024 to 11 October 2026 nothing has settled the Collatz conjecture or moved its core quantity in a way specialists have accepted. The window's largest event is the CollatzLean 'disproof' (repository dated 25 July 2026). The postmortem describes it as 'produced with AI assistance' without naming a model, and I found no account from the author that names one. Lean's kernel and the separate nanoda checker both accepted it, but de Moura's postmortem (1 August 2026) shows it exploits a kernel soundness bug that makes False provable, and Paulson's post (30 July 2026) reached the same verdict; Tao's 9 October 2026 post calls it an illicit disproof. Lean 4.32.2 fixed the bug on 28 July. I have recorded the invalidity verdict with its sources; whether the event counts toward the problem's status is left to the later pass. Partial results in the window, all unrefereed or conditional where I could check, are: Chang's two March 2026 preprints (unconditional density and measure results; the pointwise gap open; the abstract of 2603.11066 names Claude 4.6 and GPT 5.4 Thinking with a contribution analysis in Section 12 that I could not read); Nwanozie's February 2026 claim of an equivalence for the 63/64 of odd integers with v2(3N+1) ≤ 6 (equivalence step not visible in the abstract); Luo's 2025 conditional relations between step counts; Inselmann's February 2024 typical-integer and average-stopping-time results; Shakibaei Asli's January 2026 near-conjugacy, which its author says does not resolve the conjecture; Angeltveit's February 2026 finite verification algorithm; and Bařina's 2025 verification to 2^71 in the Journal of Supercomputing. Williams (July 2026) discloses a Claude Opus 4.8 model used in drafting, but the paper states its results are independent of the conjecture. The wrc-lean repository (dated only by a 23 September 2026 check run) discloses ChatGPT and Codex in writing a Lean proof of a residue bound restricted to trajectories that already reach 1; it says it does not prove termination. The many self-published 'proofs' (Duan, Diedrich, Zaman, Omran, Nwankpa, Wey, Kleinnijenhuis, Di Gruso, Lavery, Halemane, and others) have no qualified public check I could find. Close calls for the later pass: (1) Whether the density-0 divergence result of Chang 2603.11066 and the almost-all results of Tao 2019 and Inselmann move a quantity the statement names. The statement is a universal claim about every n, and these bound the measure of exceptions rather than settling them; the DEEP_DIVE §2.1 abc analogy suggests the exception set is the conjecture's own quantity, so both readings are live. (2) Whether AI involvement in Chang 2603.11066 is load-bearing: the abstract credits the models with a contribution share, but the phase-by-phase attribution in Section 12, which would decide it, could not be read. (3) Whether the AI-disclosed wrc-lean formalization is load-bearing for a Lean result it proves, which it is, but the result is restricted to terminating trajectories and so does not touch the statement. (4) Whether the June 2026 OpenAI claim exists at all; I could not find the primary article.
competing_reading: For Chang 2603.11066 and Tao 2019: the strongest case that these count is that they reduce the conjecture's exception set to measure zero or a diverging bound, which is the same kind of bound the DEEP_DIVE §2.1 abc example says moves the conjecture's own quantity. Against it, the statement asks about every n, and an exception set of density zero still allows infinitely many failures, and the 'divergent starting points' result is about measure, not about any single orbit. For the CollatzLean event: the strongest case that it counts as a disproof is that Lean accepted it under two independent kernels for about a week and the author called it a disproof; against it, the postmortem and Paulson show that acceptance rests on a soundness bug, so the claimed existence is not established. For AI attribution in Chang 2603.11066: the strongest case for load-bearing involvement is that the authors name the models in the abstract and assign them 37% and 30% of the work on a sample; against it, the abstract says the contribution analysis is in Section 12, which I could not read, and the shares may cover drafting rather than mathematics. For wrc-lean: the strongest case for load-bearing AI is that the README says substantial parts of the Lean formalisation were generated by ChatGPT and Codex, and the Lean theorem is the whole of the repository's claim; against it, the theorem is restricted to trajectories already reaching 1 and so the result does not bear on the statement.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Chang 2603.11066 Section 12, especially 12.3 'What the LLMs contributed', and the contribution table, to decide whether the models produced mathematics the result depends on. (2) A statement from xrchz (Ramana Kumar) on which tool produced the CollatzLean repository, and the Lean Zulip thread on issue #14576; the postmortem and secondary sources say 'AI assistance' without a model. (3) The first public posting date and author of the wrc-lean repository, and whether the Luo journal version (reported as published online 6 August 2026) exists. (4) Full text of Bařina (Springer), the Williams 2607.01718 disclosure in the PDF, and the Nwanozie equivalence step. (5) A refereed acceptance, or an expert write-up, of any claimed proof on the list, and any retraction or correction of the CollatzLean repo by its author. (6) A primary source for the June 2026 OpenAI claim, or the Ars Technica article it cites.

event.what_happened: Manuel Inselmann posted 'An approximation of the Collatz map and a lower bound for the average total stopping time' (arXiv 2402.03276, v1 5 Feb 2024; v3 13 Aug 2024). Its results concern typical integers and averages; the paper states they are meaningful only if the conjecture holds, and does not prove it.
event.delivers: Unconditional: for almost all m, the trajectory stays near the envelope (√3/2)^k m^(1±ε) up to k about 6.952 log m; for almost all m, the minimum T_min(m) ≤ m^ε for any ε>0, improving Korec; liminf of the average total stopping time over m ≤ x, normalised by x log x, is at least 2 / log(4/3). Conditional: if τ(m) = O(log m) for all m, that average converges to the same constant.
event.remains: Every starting integer reaching 1; the results cover typical integers and averages only.
event.direction: Toward the conjecture in density and average senses; not the conjecture.

judgement.why: The statement is a single universal claim. Results about how often orbits behave (Terras, Korec, Krasikov–Lagarias, Tao) and minimum cycle-length results (Simons–de Weger, Hercher) are answered as bound, since they move a proportion or a smallest-possible-counterexample size and leave the question open. Inselmann's natural-density improvement of Korec's exponent is the one bound after the snapshot. The density results in Chang 2603.11066 (density-0 divergence, almost-all convergence) were already known from Terras and Tao. What is new there is a spectral-gap framework and a diagnosis of why the problem resists proof, so I answered none rather than bound. That was the closest call. If it were a bound, its AI role, assisted on the abstract's co-production credit, would enter at the progress tier. Reductions, frameworks, conditional results and verification algorithms are none. Bařina's check up to 2^71 and the random-sample checks are instances. The Bouhamidi families and antihydra are variants. The CollatzLean disproof is knocked down by the kernel-bug postmortem. Its AI involvement is unnamed and its systems list is empty, so its AI role is none. The many self-published proof claims, and the uncorroborated OpenAI report, each show several F10 signals and are not_credible. wrc-lean is AI-generated, but it proves nothing about termination.
judgement.doubts: Chang 2603.11066's Section 12 was not read, so its AI role (assisted) rests on the abstract's co-production statement alone. It is moot under scope none. Whether the near-universal density results count as bounds on this statement is a judgement call; I treated measure of exceptions as a bound quantity throughout. Hercher's journal acceptance is taken as digestion despite the corrigendum. The Bouhamidi HAL 2024 entry gives only a year, so its date is null.
